title: Remembrance with breath
hookLine: simran is remembering the Name; here we let the breath carry it

lines: THE ONE THING YOU NEVER LEAVE BEHIND.
cards: What do you carry everywhere without trying? Keys, most days. A phone, almost always.
A worry or two. Every one of them has been left behind somewhere at least once: on a counter, in a cab, in a coat pocket. Except one.
Your breath has never stayed home. It goes with you to the office, into the car, into a hospital bed, into sleep. It doesn't need a gurdwara or a book or a quiet room.
On day fourteen, naam japna, keeping the name, was one of your first words. Now, a hundred and thirteen days later, the path comes back to it, slowly, for a whole week.

teach.b: Naam is the Name: not just a word for God, but God's presence, the truth the Name points to. Simran is remembering, from an old word meaning to call to mind. Naam simran: remembering the Name.
It's the third pillar you met on day fourteen, naam japna, and Sikhs call it the heart of the whole path. Seva gets the hands ready. Kirtan gets the voice and the ear ready.
Simran is where it all turns inward. Guru Arjan opens the Sukhmani, the hymn of peace, with it.
In paraphrase: remember, keep on remembering, and find peace; the troubles of the body and the mind will leave. Again and again the Guru Granth Sahib pairs remembering with breathing.

The Gurus speak of remembering God with every breath and every bite, so that no breath goes by empty. That's why this week joins simran to the breath. The breath is always there, so the remembering can always be there.

It's slow, so it slows the mind. And it's honest: you can't breathe yesterday or tomorrow, only now. Some Sikhs sit for long hours of simran before dawn, in the time the Gurus called amrit vela, the ambrosial hours.
Others remember in short moments through the day: at a red light, in a waiting room, before picking up the phone. Both are simran. No technique yet, no special words.
Just the breath, and the Name held gently alongside it, however you understand it. Tomorrow, a way to give each breath its word.

how: Sikhs practice naam simran by repeating and meditating on the Name, often Waheguru, both in the early morning hours called amrit vela and in short moments throughout the day.

o: remembering God's Name, held in the mind
thinking hard to solve a problem
reading the scripture from start to end

games.q: what's inside the word — tap the pairs.

s: simran can only be done sitting in a gurdwara
Sikhs remember at dawn and in short moments through the day: a red light, a waiting room.
the Gurus pair remembering God with the breath
remember with every breath and every bite, so no breath goes by empty.
naam just means a word for God
it points to God's presence and truth, not only a word.

games.q: you've only got two minutes and a busy mind. you want to practice naam simran. what does today suggest?
o: wait until you have an hour free before dawn.
slow your breath and hold the Name alongside it.
read as many hymns as possible in two minutes.
games.why: the breath is always there, so the remembering can always be there. short moments count as simran too.

practice: Sit upright with your hands resting and your eyes closed or soft, and just notice the breath, in and out; then let it slow a little, longer on the way in, longer on the way out.
With each breath, let the Name be there in the background, the way a candle is there in a room. When your mind wanders, and it will, come back to the next breath.

wordCard.voice: Naam simran. Remembering the Name: the heart of Sikh practice, and this week, carried on the breath.

orig.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi script: remembering the Name.

carryVoice: Your line: breath and name. The breath never stays home. One hundred twenty days now.
